title: Letters Signed With a Black Hand
bigQuestion: How can a community stand up to criminals who prey on their own neighbors?

story.title: A Letter Under the Bakery Door
story.kicker: One morning in Chicago, a baker finds a letter with no name, only a black handprint and a demand for money.
paragraphs: Early one morning, around 1908, a baker unlocks his shop in an Italian neighborhood of Chicago. The ovens are still cold. On the floor, just inside the door, lies an envelope. Someone slid it under the door in the night. This baker is not one real person. He stands for many shopkeepers whose stories appeared in newspapers of those years. We will call him Salvatore.

Salvatore opens the letter. It is written in Italian. There is no name at the bottom. There is only a drawing of a hand, inked in black. The letter demands money. It tells him where to leave it. It warns him to tell no one. It says harm will come to his shop or his family if he refuses.

Salvatore came to America to work hard and build a better life. Now he has a hard choice. He could pay and hope the letters stop. He could go to the police, but few officers speak Italian, and he is not sure they will help. Or he could talk to his neighbors. Then he might learn that he is not the only one who got a letter.

In the years after 1900, many families like Salvatore's faced this same choice. Most Italian immigrants were not criminals. They were the targets. This chapter tells how some of them, along with a few determined police officers, decided that fear would not have the last word.
story.think: If you were Salvatore, who would you want to talk to first about the letter, and why?

lessons.title: Letters That Demanded Money
lessons.mainIdea: Black Hand letters were threats sent to get money, a crime called extortion.
reading: Picture a grocer in New York in 1905. He opens a letter with no name. At the bottom are scary drawings: a hand, a dagger, maybe a skull. The letter says to pay a large sum or something terrible will happen. Letters like this were signed with a black hand. People began calling the crime itself the Black Hand.

Getting money from someone by threatening them has a name. It is called *extortion*. The Black Hand letters were extortion. They were also *anonymous*, which means the writer did not give a name. Not knowing who sent a threat made it feel even scarier. The victim could not tell if the writer was a stranger or someone down the street.

The term Black Hand was first used in New York around 1903. Letters like these spread to Chicago, New Orleans, Pittsburgh and other cities. They were most common from about 1903 to 1915. By about 1920 they had mostly faded away. Newspapers of the time printed many of the letters, so historians can study them today.

words.d: getting money from someone by threatening to hurt them or their property
sent or done without giving a name

lessons.title: A Method, Not One Gang
lessons.mainIdea: The Black Hand was a way of committing a crime, used by many small gangs, not one big secret society.
reading: In 1909, a New York police leader named Arthur Woods wrote a magazine article called "The Problem of the Black Hand." Woods was a deputy commissioner in the New York Police Department. Many readers believed the Black Hand was one huge secret *organization* with a leader and members in many cities. Woods argued that this was not true.

Woods explained that the Black Hand was a *method*. Many small gangs, not connected to each other, used the same trick. Some senders were simply copycats. They read about Black Hand letters in the newspaper and decided to try it themselves. The black hand drawing worked because it made a small gang seem big and powerful.

Historians today mostly agree with Woods. They find no proof of one Black Hand society that ran everything. This matters. A rumor about a giant secret group can make people more afraid than they need to be. It can also make them suspect a whole community. Sorting out what is proven from what is rumor is one way to fight fear.

words.d: a group of people with a structure, leaders and a shared purpose
someone who copies another person's actions, often a crime they heard about
a way of doing something

lessons.title: Neighbors Preying on Neighbors
lessons.mainIdea: Most victims of the Black Hand were Italian immigrants, targeted by criminals from their own communities.
reading: Between about 1880 and 1920, millions of Italians moved to the United States. They were immigrants, people who move to a new country to live. Many settled in city neighborhoods with other families from Italy. They opened bakeries, groceries, barbershops and small banks. Many worked long hours to save money and send some home.

Black Hand criminals looked for people like these. They mostly wrote to other Italian immigrants. They knew which shopkeepers had savings. They knew newcomers might not speak English well. They also knew many newcomers did not trust police, because officials back home had not always been fair. To *prey on* people means to hunt them as targets. These criminals preyed on their own neighbors.

This is the most important fact in this chapter. The Black Hand was not "what Italians did." Most Italian immigrants were the victims, not the criminals. The criminals were a small number of people. Historians such as Humbert Nelli, who studied Italians in Chicago, make this point clearly.

words.d: a person who moves to a new country to live
to hunt or target people in order to harm or cheat them
a person who is harmed by a crime or other wrong

lessons.title: When Fear Keeps People Quiet
lessons.mainIdea: Extortion works only when victims stay silent, so speaking up is how it is broken.
reading: Think about what a Black Hand gang needed. It needed people to pay. It also needed people to stay quiet. If victims told the police, the gang could be caught. So the letters always warned: tell no one. The criminals counted on *silence* to protect them.

Sometimes, when a shopkeeper refused to pay, a gang set off a small bomb at the shop or home. Newspapers reported these attacks. The goal was to scare the whole street, not just one person. When neighbors saw a damaged shop, some decided it was safer to pay. The fear spread further than the harm itself.

But silence also had a weak point. When one victim spoke up, others often came forward too. A *witness* is a person who tells what they saw or know, often in court. Every witness made the gang weaker. That is why the people who spoke up, and the people who protected them, are the real heroes of this history.

words.d: not speaking; here, not telling police or others about a crime
a person who tells what they saw or know, often in a court

lessons.title: A Detective Who Spoke Italian
lessons.mainIdea: Joseph Petrosino, an Italian-born New York detective, led a squad that could talk to victims in their own language.
reading: Joseph Petrosino was born in 1860 in southern Italy. He came to New York as a boy. As a young man he joined the New York Police Department. At that time, very few officers spoke Italian. Petrosino did. He could talk with shopkeepers, workers and families in the way they spoke at home.

Petrosino became a *detective*, a police officer who investigates crimes to find out who did them. Around 1906, he was put in charge of a special *squad*, a small team, of Italian-speaking officers. People called it the Italian Squad. He later reached the rank of lieutenant.

Language mattered. A victim who could explain a threat in Italian, to an officer who understood, was more likely to come forward. Petrosino's squad arrested many extortionists. He also wanted Americans to see that Italian immigrants were fighting crime, not causing it. He was an Italian American standing up for other Italian Americans.

words.d: a police officer who investigates crimes to find out who did them
a small team of police officers or soldiers with one job

lessons.title: Records, Not Guns
lessons.mainIdea: Petrosino believed that official records from Italy could remove extortionists from America.
reading: Petrosino noticed something about many extortionists. Some had already been convicted of crimes in Italy. They had kept that past hidden when they came to America. A *criminal record* is an official list of crimes a person has been convicted of. If Petrosino could get those records, he could prove who these men really were.

Under American law, some immigrants who hid a criminal past could be deported, or sent back to the country they came from. So Petrosino's best tool was paper, not a gun. In early 1909 he sailed to Italy on a secret trip. His plan was to gather criminal records from Italian courts and police.

The trip was supposed to stay secret. But news of it leaked and was printed in a New York newspaper. People who wanted to stop him may have learned he was coming. Petrosino went ahead anyway. He traveled to Sicily, the island where many of the records he wanted were kept.

words.d: an official list of the crimes a person has been convicted of
to send a person out of a country, back to where they came from

lessons.title: Piazza Marina, 1909
lessons.mainIdea: Petrosino was killed in Palermo in 1909, and no one was ever convicted of his murder.
reading: On the evening of 12 March 1909, Joseph Petrosino was in Piazza Marina, a square in Palermo, Sicily. Shots were fired, and he was killed. He had been in Sicily only a short time. He died doing the work he believed in: gathering proof.

Police in Italy investigated. The chief *suspect*, the person they most believed was responsible, was a Sicilian crime figure named Vito Cascio Ferro. But he was never *convicted*. That means no court ever found him guilty. No one else was convicted either. The case remains officially unsolved.

Here is how a careful historian sorts it. Documented: Petrosino was shot dead in Piazza Marina on 12 March 1909. Documented: no one was convicted. Disputed: who gave the order. Police files and later claims point to Cascio Ferro, but that evidence was never tested in a trial. We can say he was the main suspect. We cannot say he was proven guilty.

words.d: a person police believe may have committed a crime
found guilty of a crime by a court
shown by records or other solid evidence

lessons.title: A City Says Goodbye
lessons.mainIdea: Huge crowds mourned Petrosino in New York, showing how many people honored his stand against the Black Hand.
reading: Petrosino's body was brought home to New York. His funeral was held on 12 April 1909, one month after his death. The streets filled with people. Many were Italian immigrants. They had lost a man who had fought for them.

How many came? Newspapers printed an *estimate*, a careful guess, not an exact count. The New York Times reported about 200,000 people. Other reports said about 250,000. No one could count every person on a crowded street, so the numbers differ. Historians give both and name who made them.

The funeral sent a message. Petrosino had been an Italian immigrant who became a police leader. The crowds showed that a huge part of the Italian community stood with him, not with the criminals. A funeral like this is also a *memorial*, a way to remember a person and what he stood for.

words.d: a careful guess at a number when an exact count is not possible
something done or built to remember a person or event

lessons.title: The White Hand Society
lessons.mainIdea: Italian Americans in Chicago formed the White Hand Society in 1907 and 1908 to fight the Black Hand.
reading: In November 1907, Italian-American community leaders in Chicago brought a plan to the Italian *consul*. A consul is an official who looks after his country's people living abroad. Their plan was a new group to fight Black Hand extortion. By early 1908, the group had an office in the Masonic Temple Building, at State and Randolph streets downtown.

They called it the White Hand Society. The name was a direct answer to the Black Hand. White stood for honesty and for acting in the open. A *society* here means an organized group of people working for a shared goal. This society was not secret. It wanted everyone to know Italian Americans were against the extortionists.

The White Hand offered rewards, money for information that helped catch criminals. It pushed police and courts to take Black Hand cases seriously. It urged victims to come forward and tell what they knew. Not every effort succeeded. But it showed that the community was organizing itself against crime.

words.d: an organized group of people working together for a shared goal
money or a prize offered for help, such as information about a crime
an official who looks after his or her country's people living in another country

lessons.title: Fighting a Stereotype Too
lessons.mainIdea: Italian Americans had to fight both real criminals and an unfair stereotype that blamed their whole community.
reading: A *stereotype* is an unfair idea that everyone in a group is the same. In the early 1900s, many Americans held a stereotype that Italians were criminals. This hurt honest families. Some landlords would not rent to them. Some bosses would not hire them. The Black Hand made this stereotype worse.

Stereotypes can lead to terrible harm. In New Orleans in 1890, the city's police chief was murdered. Some Italian men were put on trial, but the trial ended without convictions. On 14 March 1891, a mob broke into the jail and killed 11 Italian men. This was a *lynching*, a killing by a mob without any trial. *Prejudice*, judging people unfairly because of their group, drove the mob.

More than a century later, in 2019, the mayor of New Orleans, LaToya Cantrell, formally apologized to Italian Americans for the lynching. Groups like the White Hand wanted to fight both dangers at once. They wanted to stop the criminals and show that the Italian community was on the side of the law.

words.d: an unfair idea that everyone in a group is the same
judging people unfairly because of the group they belong to
a killing by a mob, without a trial

lessons.title: How the Black Hand Faded
lessons.mainIdea: By about 1920 Black Hand letters had mostly stopped, and historians weigh several reasons why.
reading: By about 1920, Black Hand letters had mostly faded away. Why? Historians give several reasons. They do not all agree on which reason mattered most. When experts weigh the same evidence differently, we call the question *contested*.

One reason is better policing. Italian-speaking officers, like Petrosino's squad, made it easier for victims to report threats. Some extortionists were arrested, convicted or deported. A second reason is *community action*. Groups like the White Hand, along with brave witnesses, broke the silence the gangs needed.

A third reason some historians give comes from a new law. In 1920, the United States banned the sale of alcohol. Selling alcohol illegally became a far bigger business than threatening shopkeepers. Some criminals may have moved into it. That story is the next chapter. The lesson of this one is clear: silence protected the Black Hand, and speaking up together weakened it.

words.d: argued about; experts weigh the evidence differently
neighbors working together to solve a shared problem
